Chapter Three: Moving Beyond Avoidance—Facing Relationship Pain Points Directly.
Even when you’ve built a relationship on honesty and vulnerability, it’s so common to run into avoidance. I mean, who really enjoys diving into the tough stuff, right? It’s natural to want to steer clear of topics that feel threatening or painful. But here’s the thing—when we dodge those issues, they don’t just disappear. They tend to fester and grow in the shadows.
Avoidance can sneak in in all sorts of ways. Maybe you change the subject when things get sensitive, or you downplay your concerns, or just pretend everything’s fine. At first, it might seem like you’re keeping the peace. But underneath that calm surface, there’s usually a buildup of frustration and unmet needs.
Let’s make this real for a second. Imagine a couple who always sidesteps talking about money because it leads to arguments. As time goes on, financial stress just keeps piling up, and both people start to feel more and more alone. The tension, even though it’s unspoken, starts leaking into other parts of the relationship. Suddenly, even tiny disagreements can feel massive.
So, how do you get past avoidance? First, it’s about noticing the signs—and understanding what it’s costing you. Are there topics you always tiptoe around? Do you ever feel like you’re carrying a silent weight? Here’s something to pay attention to: those hidden issues don’t just vanish. They wait, and they grow.
Facing pain points head-on isn’t about picking a fight. It’s about showing up with a little courage and a lot of curiosity. Think of it as an invitation to really understand each other, even when things get uncomfortable. Ask questions, stay open, and let yourself sit with the awkwardness for a bit. It’s tough, but it’s worth it.
Want a practical way to get started? Here are a few simple steps:
First, name the issue. Just say what’s been avoided—without blaming or accusing.
Next, invite a real dialogue. Instead of trying to “win,” let your partner know you genuinely want to hear their side.
And finally, pick a good time. Don’t bring up the tough stuff in the middle of an argument or when someone’s distracted. Find a moment when you can both be present and focused.
Here’s a helpful analogy: think of relationship pain points like weeds in a garden. Ignoring them won’t make them go away. It just gives them more space to take root and spread. But if you address them early, you prevent those little weeds from turning into something much bigger.
And remember, not every pain point needs an instant fix. Some things take time and a few conversations to work through. The real goal isn’t to be perfect—it’s to make steady progress. Just being willing to come back to the table, even when things feel uncertain, is huge.
Over time, this practice builds real resilience. You start to trust that you can face challenges together, not just alone. And every small, honest conversation adds to the sense that your relationship can handle whatever comes next.
